blocks.p: After [Validating and Normalizing](piece:validating-and-normalizing) comes the dual cognitive skill of Imagery & Invitation. Imagery & Invitation intentionally allow mild to moderate defensive activation through thought, while you also do something else. Imagery uses your imagination to craft a picture of your emotions. Invitation permits that emotion to coexist with you instead of rejecting it.

There are two reasons to practice Imagery & Invitation. First, to reduce the friction of resisting defense. Whatever you're feeling is already there, so we are continuing to pay attention to it. Second, to practice inviting tolerable defense, which is direct preparation for the more advanced somatic skills, like [Balancing and Pendulating](piece:balancing-and-pendulating).
Giving the defense an image can happen in two ways:

ul: You intentionally assign one.
You let one emerge spontaneously.

blocks.p: Both methods work, but spontaneous emergence is preferable. There's no right or wrong image, and I recommend not judging whatever appears. If you intentionally create one, use it. If something shows up on its own, go with that.
To help yourself create an Image to invite, ask yourself what it looks like, where it is, and what it's doing.
What does the emotion look like?

ul: "Anger is a flame."
"Sad is a sack of potatoes."
"Anxiety is an electric bolt."

blocks.p: Where is the emotion?

ul: "Anger is a flame in front of me."
"Sad is a sack of potatoes in my gut."
"Anxiety is an electric bolt all around."

blocks.p: What is the emotion doing?

ul: "Anger is a flame in front of me, bouncing."
"Sad is a sack of potatoes in my gut, pulling down."
"Anxiety is an electric bolt all around, jittery."

blocks.p: Once you have the image, Invite it to stay with you. Not rejecting. Ultimately, you're allowing it. You're giving the emotion explicit permission to remain present. At this point, not all of it and not at a very deep level. For now, we're staying in the cognitive realm, not venturing further into the body.

However, Inviting also inherently means that you're allowing it to join you as you do something else. Go for a walk, stretch, lie down, use your senses, read a book, work out, paint, make a phone call, or do the dishes. The "something else" doesn't need to be elaborate; it just needs to shift some of your attention outward while the emotion stays at this cognitive level. You're not ignoring the emotion; you're beginning to coexist with it.

If Inviting it feels too overwhelming, it's okay to imagine placing the emotion somewhere respectful, like on a shelf, off to the side, or in another room. Tell it you'll return when you're ready. That's not failure. When you're ready, try again.

blocks.why: Invitation works best from a firm anchor. This practice anchors you first.

blocks.p: Putting the skills together:

ul: Validate: "I feel anxious."
Normalize: "I feel anxious, which makes sense based on my work stress."
Imagery and invitation: "Anxiety has permission to be with me. It looks like a jittery little bird and can sit on my shoulder while I take a walk around the block before emails."
Validate: "I feel unmotivated."
Normalize: "I feel unmotivated, and that makes sense based on living in chronic shutdown."
Imagery and invitation: "Unmotivated looks like a wet washrag. I'll hang it in my shower and let it be there while I lie on the floor and wiggle my toes."
Validate: "I feel angry."
Normalize: "I feel angry, and that makes sense based on Justin prompting me to look at my feelings, which I don't like doing."
Imagery and invitation: "Angry looks like a roaring flame superpower all around me, and it can be here as I get in my car to get the dang groceries done even though I really don't want to."

blocks.p: Imagery & Invitation remains primarily cognitive. If you find Imagery & Invitation easy, you're probably ready to move from cognitive to somatic and on to the next skills. You can revisit Imagery & Invitation anytime you need, such as when unexpected emotions come up during meditation, when something surprises you during your day, or when you just want to practice being present with what is there.

Think of Imagery & Invitation as a temporary stepping stone. These two skills are not meant to be a permanent part of your meditative practice. Instead, as they become easier for you to use, you will move past them and focus on [Balancing and Pendulating](piece:balancing-and-pendulating). You can always return to Imagery & Invitation whenever you need to.
"No image comes to mind for my emotion."

That's okay. Not every emotion will produce imagery immediately. If nothing arises after a few moments and you can tolerate the emotion, move to Invitation without the Imagery step. You can also try narrowing the potential answers, such as "If this emotion were a rock, what kind would it be?" or "What type of cloud is this emotion?"
"The image that comes up is disturbing or scary."

If the image itself triggers defensiveness, you might be working with a defense that's too intense right now. Return to safety anchoring. Try this skill with milder defense first: irritation instead of rage, unease instead of terror.
"I can invite the emotion, but it's overwhelming."

You're likely not anchored firmly enough in safety before inviting. Check your safety level: are you at 3 or more out of 5? If not, spend more time with [Cue to Anchor](piece:cue-to-anchor) before attempting Invitation. Also, invite the emotion to be with you while you do something highly sensory (holding your safety object, feeling the breeze) or active (walking, pushups) rather than something neutral.
"I don't know what to do when inviting the emotion."

Keep it simple. The "something else" you do while inviting can be: taking one mindful breath, feeling your safety cue for 10 seconds, looking around your environment and naming three things you see, or getting out of the house. It can even be chores you planned for the day.
Imagery uses your imagination to create a visual for your emotions (internal or external), and Invitation respectfully allows that emotion to be present while you engage in another activity.
Imagery & Invitation are a temporary stepping stone to connect with a deeper felt sense of defense.
If Inviting an emotion feels too overwhelming, you can temporarily set it aside with respect and plan to return to it when you're ready, gradually building your capacity to handle it.

Choose one emotion you have [Validated and Normalized](piece:validating-and-normalizing). Give it either an internal image (inside your body) or an external image (outside of you). Don't force the image; simply observe what your mind naturally creates.

Then invite it to be with you as you do something else, like taking a deliberate breath, feeling your safety cue, looking around your environment, or taking a short walk. Practice allowing the emotion to coexist (as an Invited Image) with your mindful present-moment connection.
If inviting feels too overwhelming, picture placing the emotion somewhere respectful (like a shelf or beside you) and tell it you'll come back when you're ready.
